results.question: `fib3` (memoised) makes the same recursive calls as `fib1`, yet runs in linear time. Why?

options.text: It makes fewer calls than `fib1` in total
options.explanation: The number of calls is about the same. What changes is how much work each repeat call does.

options.text: There are only n distinct subproblems, F(0) to F(n), and each is computed once; every other call is a lookup
options.explanation: Right. Count distinct subproblems, not calls. The call tree is just as bushy, but almost every node does no work.

options.text: It replaces recursion with a loop, and loops are always linear
options.explanation: `fib3` is still recursive. It is the notebook that removes the repeated work.

options.text: Memoisation makes each call cheaper by a constant factor
options.explanation: A constant factor cannot turn an exponential into a linear cost.

results.chosenAnswer: There are only n distinct subproblems, F(0) to F(n), and each is computed once; every other call is a lookup
results.correctAnswer: There are only n distinct subproblems, F(0) to F(n), and each is computed once; every other call is a lookup
workedSolution: `fib1` recomputes each `F(k)` many times because nothing records an answer.
`fib3` checks a notebook first and writes to it after, so `F(k)` is computed once.
There are only `n + 1` different questions, each answered once at constant cost, so the total is linear.
The calls are still made, but almost all of them are a single lookup.

results.question: You buy a machine twice as fast. Roughly how much larger an input can `fib1` handle in the same time, given that its work multiplies by about 1.618 per extra unit of `n`?

options.explanation: It buys a little, about 1.4 extra values of `n`, but no more.
That is what a linear algorithm would give you. `fib1` is exponential.

options.text: About 1.4 larger, i.e. n grows by roughly 1.44
options.explanation: Right. You can afford `log_φ 2 ≈ 1.44` extra multiplications by φ. Hardware barely moves an exponential.
Doubling the speed buys one factor of 2, and 1.618 fits into 2 only about 1.44 times.

results.chosenAnswer: About 1.4 larger, i.e. n grows by roughly 1.44
results.correctAnswer: About 1.4 larger, i.e. n grows by roughly 1.44
workedSolution: Doubling speed lets you afford one extra factor of 2 in work.
Each extra unit of `n` costs a factor of `φ ≈ 1.618`.
The number of extra units is `log_φ 2 = ln 2 / ln 1.618 ≈ 0.693 / 0.481 ≈ 1.44`.
So `n` grows by about 1.4, not by a factor of 2.

results.question: Which pair of witnesses does NOT prove that 3n + 7 = O(n)?

results.question: Which statement about 3n is FALSE?

options.explanation: True: for any c > 0, 3n ≤ c·n² once n ≥ 3/c.

options.text: O applies to time and Ω applies to space

options.text: Nothing: that is what the symbols mean

results.question: Production sorting libraries switch to insertion sort for very small arrays, even though mergesort is O(n log n) and insertion sort is O(n²). Which idea from Week 1 explains this?

options.text: Insertion sort is Θ(n log n) on small arrays

options.text: Mergesort is only correct for large arrays

results.question: An algorithm runs one phase costing Θ(n log n) and then a second phase costing Θ(n). What is the total?

options.explanation: Running phases in sequence adds their costs. It does not multiply them.
That is the smaller phase. The total cannot be smaller than the bigger phase.
Neither phase is logarithmic, and the sum cannot be smaller than either part.

results.correctAnswer: Θ(n log n)
workedSolution: Sequential phases add: `n log n + n`.
For non-negative `f, g`: `max{f, g} ≤ f + g ≤ 2·max{f, g}`, so the sum is `Θ` of the larger.
For `n ≥ 2`, `n log n ≥ n`, so the total is `Θ(n log n)`.
